Waterborne disease: tables and bibliographic integrity in a CDC surveillance report

Source: vignettes/waterborne-disease.Rmd
waterborne-disease.Rmd
library(bst260projhelp)

This vignette works through the CDC’s 2021 Annual Waterborne Disease Surveillance Report (the WBDOSS summary), bundled with the package:

pdf <- bst260_example("2021_Annual_Waterborne_Disease_Surveillance_Report.pdf")
pdftools::pdf_info(pdf)[c("pages", "created", "version")]
#> $pages
#> [1] 26
#> 
#> $created
#> [1] "2024-04-12 11:08:51 EDT"
#> 
#> $version
#> [1] "1.7"

As the original data-raw/waterborne/README.txt for this project put it: the underlying question is whether results pulled from this single annual report are consistent with the longer 1971-2023 WBDOSS resource studied elsewhere in the course, which makes getting the extraction right – not just plausible-looking – the point of this vignette.

Information transformation: two kinds of PDF table

Where does each table start?

pdf_caption_index(pdf)
#>    page    table
#> 1     2  Table 1
#> 2     5  Table 2
#> 3     6  Table 3
#> 4     8  Table 4
#> 5     9  Table 5
#> 6     9  Table 6
#> 7    10  Table 7
#> 8    10  Table 8
#> 9    12  Table 9
#> 10   15 Table 10
#> 11   17 Table 11
#> 12   18 Table 12
#> 13   19 Table 13
#> 14   19 Table 14
#> 15   22 Table 15
#> 16   24 Table 16

Tables with no wrapped cells: a simple line-by-line read

Tables 1 and 3 are short enough, and typeset simply enough, that each row is a single text line: a label followed by one or more count (percent) pairs, ending in a “Total” row. pdf_read_count_pct_table() reads this layout directly off pdftools::pdf_text(), with no need for word coordinates:

tab1 <- pdf_read_count_pct_table(
  pdf, page = 3, header_pat = "^\\s*(Water\\s+)?Exposure",
  col_names = c("outbreaks", "cases", "hosp", "deaths")
)
tab1
#>          label outbreaks_n outbreaks_pct cases_n cases_pct hosp_n hosp_pct
#> 1 Recreational          32            62     284        56     37       36
#> 2     Drinking          15            29     214        42     56       54
#> 3        Other           1             2       2         0      2        2
#> 4      Unknown           4             8      11         2      9        9
#> 5        Total          52           100     511       100    104      100
#>   deaths_n deaths_pct
#> 1        1         10
#> 2        7         70
#> 3        0         NA
#> 4        2         20
#> 5       10        100

tab3 <- pdf_read_count_pct_table(
  pdf, page = 6, header_pat = "^Setting\\s+N",
  col_names = c("outbreaks", "cases")
)
tab3
#>                           label outbreaks_n outbreaks_pct cases_n cases_pct
#> 1                   Hotel/Motel          13            25     116        23
#> 2  Hospital/Healthcare Facility           9            17      38         7
#> 3     Outdoor Recreational Area           6            12      64        13
#> 4                         Beach           5            10      23         5
#> 5               Apartment/Condo           4             8      31         6
#> 6    Club (Requires Membership)           3             6      12         2
#> 7            Camp/Cabin Setting           2             4      99        19
#> 8        Community/Municipality           2             4      68        13
#> 9     School/College/University           2             4      32         6
#> 10     Subdivision/Neighborhood           2             4      13         3
#> 11                      Unknown           2             4       6         1
#> 12            Private Residence           1             2       5         1
#> 13                    Ship/Boat           1             2       4         1
#> 14                        Total          52           100     511       100

The report prints its own totals, so we can check the extraction against them directly – the kind of check worth automating as a stopifnot() rather than eyeballing once and trusting forever:

stopifnot(
  sum(tab3$outbreaks_n[tab3$label != "Total"]) == 52,
  sum(tab3$cases_n[tab3$label != "Total"]) == 511
)

Tables with wrapped cells: word-geometry extraction

Table 8 (treated recreational water outbreaks, pages 11-12) is harder: columns are centred rather than left-aligned, and cells like etiology or jurisdiction can wrap across several lines, so a line-by-line read would scramble rows. pdf_read_wide_wrapped_table() instead assigns every word to its nearest column-header centre and then to the row (anchored on the first column) that it vertically belongs to:

h <- function(prefix, k = 1) c(prefix, k)
cols8 <- list(
  Jurisdiction = list(h("Jurisdiction")),
  Month        = list(h("Month")),
  Status       = list(h("Status")),
  Etiology     = list(h("Etiology", 2)),       # "Etiology" appears twice in the header
  Cases        = list(h("Cases")),
  Hosp         = list(h("Hospitalizati")),      # poppler splits "Hospitalizations"
  Deaths       = list(h("Deaths")),
  Venue        = list(h("Water", 1), h("Venue(s)")),
  Setting      = list(h("Water", 2), h("Setting"))
)
tab8 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(11:12, function(p) pdf_read_wide_wrapped_table(pdf, p, cols8)))
tab8[c("Cases", "Hosp", "Deaths")] <- lapply(tab8[c("Cases", "Hosp", "Deaths")], as.integer)
tab8$Setting <- sub("/(Neig|Mun|Cond|U) ", "/\\1", tab8$Setting)  # repair a poppler line-split
nrow(tab8)  # expect 22
#> [1] 22
dtab(tab8)

Both extraction strategies are generic: neither function hard-codes anything about waterborne disease, so the same calls work on the gun policy report’s tables – see vignette("gun-legislation") – by supplying that document’s own page numbers and column layout.

Bibliographic integrity: a numbered (Vancouver-style) reference list

Unlike the RAND report, this document cites by number – "(1)", "(2)" – against a short, two-entry reference list on page 25:

refs_raw <- vancouver_ref_entries(pdf, page = 25)
refs_raw
#>                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1 
#> "Collier SA, Deng L, Adam EA, et al. Estimate of Burden and Direct Healthcare Cost of Infectious Waterborne Disease in the United States. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2021;27(1):140-149. doi:10.3201/eid2701.190676." 
#>                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2 
#>                                                      "Information about Public Water Systems. 2021 11/10/2021 [cited 2021 11/22]; Available from: https://www.epa.gov/dwreginfo/information-about-public-water-systems."

Each entry has its own shape (a journal article vs. a web resource), so each is parsed with the matching function:

refs <- list(
  Collier2021 = vancouver_parse_article(refs_raw[["1"]], 1),
  EPA2021PWS  = vancouver_parse_web(refs_raw[["2"]], 2)
)
str(refs, max.level = 1)
#> List of 2
#>  $ Collier2021:List of 10
#>  $ EPA2021PWS :List of 9

Most of the report’s real evidentiary sources, though, are surveillance systems (NORS, the NORS Dashboard, reporting forms) named in the Methods and Conclusions sections rather than cited by number. Treating these as if they weren’t sources at all would understate what the report actually depends on, so they are curated by hand as @misc entries (their URLs taken from the PDF’s own hyperlink annotations) and combined with the parsed numbered references and the report’s own “Suggested Citation” for itself:

cdc <- "{Centers for Disease Control and Prevention}"
curated <- list(
  Lawinger2023WBDOSS = list(
    type = "techreport",
    author = "Lawinger, H. and Hlavsa, M. and Miko, S. and Kunz, J. and Thuneibat, M. and Gerdes, M. and Gleason, M. and Roberts, V.",
    title = "Waterborne Disease and Outbreak Surveillance System ({WBDOSS}) Summary Report, {United States}, 2021",
    institution = "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, CDC", address = "Atlanta, Georgia", year = "2023",
    annote = "Citation text from the report's own 'Suggested Citation' (p. 26)."
  ),
  CDCNORS = list(
    type = "misc", author = cdc, title = "National Outbreak Reporting System ({NORS})",
    url = "https://www.cdc.gov/nors/index.html",
    note = "Web-based platform used by jurisdictions to report outbreaks since 2009"
  ),
  CDCNORSDashboard = list(
    type = "misc", author = cdc, title = "{NORS} Dashboard",
    url = "https://www.cdc.gov/nors/data/dashboard/index.html",
    note = "2021 data in the report: outbreaks reported through NORS as of 19 January 2023; later pulls may differ"
  )
)
all_refs <- c(refs, curated)

That’s the full setup this package’s bibliography tools need: parsed numbered references plus any hand-curated entries, combined into one named list keyed by citation key. From here on, only the final rendered bibliography is shown, not the construction code.

Cross-checking the numbered citations

vancouver_find_numeric_citations() scans the whole document for text matching the "word (N)" citation pattern, so the two entries in the reference list can be checked against where they’re actually used – a cheap guard against a reference that was added (or removed) from the list without updating the citation, or vice versa. Each hit below is itself a link down to the entry it cites, and carries its own anchor id so that entry can link back up to this exact page:

nc <- vancouver_find_numeric_citations(pdf, max_ref = length(refs_raw))
num_to_key <- c(`1` = "Collier2021", `2` = "EPA2021PWS")
nc_keys <- strsplit(nc$numbers, ",")
cite_id <- Map(function(ks, i) paste0("cite-", num_to_key[ks], "-", i), nc_keys, seq_len(nrow(nc)))
nc$reference <- vapply(seq_along(nc_keys), function(i) {
  paste(bib_cite_link(num_to_key[nc_keys[[i]]], label = nc_keys[[i]], id = cite_id[[i]]), collapse = ", ")
}, "")
cited_at <- split(unlist(cite_id), unlist(lapply(nc_keys, function(ks) num_to_key[ks])))
dtab(nc[c("page", "cited", "reference")], escape = FALSE)

Both numbered citations – one on page 1, one on page 17 – are accounted for in the two-entry reference list, which is the bibliographic-integrity claim this section set out to check.

The rendered bibliography

Each entry links to its DOI on doi.org when Crossref’s own parsed DOI was captured in the reference text; failing that, to its plain url when one is known (true of every curated entry, cited by its web page rather than a DOI); and is explicitly marked no DOI in either case when no DOI was found. The small &uarr; after Collier2021 and EPA2021PWS links back up to the page that cited them, found above – the curated entries have no such link, since they’re named in the report’s prose rather than cited by number:

cat(vancouver_bibliography_html(all_refs, cited_at), sep = "\n")
  1. Collier, S. A. and Deng, L. and Adam, E. A. and others. Estimate of Burden and Direct Healthcare Cost of Infectious Waterborne Disease in the United States. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2021;27(1):140–149. https://doi.org/10.3201/eid2701.190676 ↑
  2. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Information about Public Water Systems. Page last updated 2021-11-10. 2021. no DOI (https://www.epa.gov/dwreginfo/information-about-public-water-systems) ↑
  3. Lawinger, H. and Hlavsa, M. and Miko, S. and Kunz, J. and Thuneibat, M. and Gerdes, M. and Gleason, M. and Roberts, V.. Waterborne Disease and Outbreak Surveillance System (WBDOSS) Summary Report, United States, 2021. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, CDC, Atlanta, Georgia. 2023. no DOI
  4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. National Outbreak Reporting System (NORS). no DOI (https://www.cdc.gov/nors/index.html)
  5. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. NORS Dashboard. no DOI (https://www.cdc.gov/nors/data/dashboard/index.html)

A caution about URLs

The curated @misc entries above point at live CDC web resources rather than fixed, versioned documents, and CDC has reorganized its site before. vancouver_check_urls() (not run here, since it requires network access) sends a HEAD request to every URL in a reference list and reports the HTTP status, as a first-pass check that a citation still resolves to something – not proof that the content hasn’t changed underneath it:

vancouver_check_urls(all_refs)
